reasoning.Student A: My goal is to be matched with my most preferred school from the "obtainable set." The obtainable set is determined by the school priorities, not my ranking. Therefore, I should rank the schools according to my true preferences. My preference is y > x > w > z. Ranking according to my true preferences guarantees that I will get the best possible outcome within my obtainable set.
reasoning.Student B:
My goal is to be matched to the best school possible according to my preference: y > x > z > w. My final match will be my favorite school from the set of schools that would accept me.

School x and z both give me the highest priority (1). This means they are both in my "obtainable set". Since x > z, I would prefer to be matched to x.

School w and y both give me priority 2. Whether they are in my obtainable set depends on other students' applications. However, since x and z are guaranteed to be in my obtainable set, I only need to consider whether y is also obtainable. If y is obtainable, I prefer y > x > z > w. If y is NOT obtainable, I prefer x > z > w.

Since most applicants seem to favor y > x > w > z, it is likely that many applicants will apply to y. This means that I might not be able to get into y because I only have priority 2 there. However, I should still rank y first, because if I *can* get in, I would prefer it.

Given that x and z are both in my obtainable set, I should rank them according to my preference. This means x > z.

Finally, I should rank w last. It is my least preferred school, and I only have priority 2 there. Even if y is not obtainable, I would still prefer x or z to w.

Therefore, my ranking should be y > x > z > w.
reasoning.Student C:
My goal is to be matched with my most preferred school from the set of schools that would accept me. My stated preferences are y > x > z > w.

The key insight is that my ranking only affects which *obtainable* school I get into. Thus, I should rank the schools in my true preference order. This ensures that if multiple schools would accept me, I get my favorite among them.

Therefore, I will rank the schools y > x > z > w.
reasoning.Student D: My goal is to maximize my chances of attending my most preferred school, y. Since my outcome is determined by my priorities and not my ranking, I want to rank the schools according to my preference: y > x > w > z. This ensures that if y is obtainable, I will get it. If y is not obtainable but x is, I will get x, and so on. Ranking the schools in any other order wouldn't change the set of schools that might accept me, but it could lead to me getting a less preferred school from the obtainable set.
